records.content_title: Measles spread to another Ohio county as cases grow
records.content: Sept. 11, 2026, 10:27 a.m. ET Ohio is experiencing its third measles outbreak of 2026, with 133 cases reported across 15 counties this year. Nationwide, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, a resurgence health experts attribute to declining vaccination rates. Ohio health officials are urging residents to get the MMR vaccine, which is 97% effective against the disease. New measles cases in Ohio have dropped from week to week amid the state's third measles outbreak of 2026. Ohio had 11 new cases in the past week, down from 15 the week before. The Ohio Department of Health is reporting 133 cases in 15 counties this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Sept. 10. That's up from 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3; 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27; 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20; 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13; and 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. Portage County confirmed its first measles case, the county Health District announced Sept. 8. At the time, no public exposure locations associated with this case had been identified. "PCHD is working closely with the Ohio Department of Health to investigate the case and identify and notify individuals who may have been exposed," the health department stated on Facebook. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released July 22 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 2,295 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Once-eradicated disease returns: Measles cases hit highest level in 35 years Measles growing in Ohio; counties reporting cases Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashtabula : 30 (three new cases as of Sept. 10) : 30 (three new cases as of Sept. 10) Cuyahoga : 3 : 3 Franklin : 7 : 7 Gallia : 3 (two new cases) : 3 (two new cases) Geauga : 33 (one new case) : 33 (one new case) Harrison : 11 (one new case) : 11 (one new case) Holmes : 7 (one new case) : 7 (one new case) Knox : 5 (one new case) : 5 (one new case) Meigs : 4 : 4 Morgan : 1 : 1 Ottawa : 1 : 1 Portage : 1 (one new case) : 1 (one new case) Trumbull : 6 (one new case) : 6 (one new case) Tuscarawas : 12 : 12 Wayne: 9 The case count reflects two previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. Pennsylvania measles deaths At least two people this year have died from measles in Pennsylvania, according to USA TODAY. Both were unvaccinated and both were infants, the Lancaster County coroner said, according to CBS News. The measles deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state Department of Health said in an Aug. 25 news release, and the first such deaths in the United States this year, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. US measles cases: 3 states battling new outbreaks. What to know Where are measles cases spreading? While Harrison County Public Health reported one case of measles as of Aug. 7, the state dashboard shows additional cases there. The Wayne County Health Department reports some of its cases are likely associated with a previously identified measles exposure event at Smokey Lane Stables, 686 Smokey Lane Road NW in Sugarcreek, on July 17. One of the Tuscarawas cases is from the same event, that county health department reports. Geauga Public Health reports that the individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. In Trumbull County, health officials report that infected individuals were at the Walmart in Liberty on July 29 and Akron Children's Mahoning Valley Emergency Department in Boardman on Aug. 2, during the time they were able to spread the virus. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. See the charts: Measles cases reach highest level in 35 years Why are measles cases on the rise? Ohio vaccination rates Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventives, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023, the most recent year available from ODH. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019 : 81.8% : 81.8% 2020 : 88.0% : 88.0% 2021 : 91.7% : 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lower overall vaccination rates, according to experts. The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report

Why is measles spreading in Central New York? topics: Measles Vaccination Outbreak MMR Health officials Utica Onondaga County New York SYRACUSE, N.Y. — Measles cases are rising across the country and public health officials in Central New York are warning the highly contagious virus could soon spread into more populated areas, including Onondaga County. The region is already seeing confirmed cases in Cayuga, Cortland and Madison counties. Measles was eradicated in the United States in 2000, but has returned, with more than 3,100 cases reported nationwide this year alone. There were two infant deaths in Pennsylvania last month and 51 measles cases reported across New York State. “It’s really not surprising at all, unfortunately, because of the number of measles cases over the last several years countrywide. And if anything, I’m quite surprised that it took this long for us to experience cases in Upstate New York,” said Onondaga County Senior Medical Director Dr. James Alexander. Dr. Alexander said vaccine skepticism at the highest levels of government has contributed to lower vaccination rates. “Certainly the narrative that’s coming out on the national level, that has not helped. There tends to be vaccine uptake that is divided on where you fall on the political spectrum. We see lower vaccine rates in the politically conservative parts of the country,” he said. Powered By 10 Sec Liverpool mom remembers daughter killed on 9/11 as a 'force of nature' Next Stay Alexander said he expects Onondaga County will eventually see cases. “I think it’s fairly likely that we will see measles cases in Onondaga County because, as you say, measles don’t know geographical boundaries and I think it’s just a matter of time,” he said. Measles is a potentially deadly respiratory disease that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Complications can include pneumonia, encephalitis and death. Dr. Alexander urged people to take the threat seriously and get vaccinated. “You can die from measles. You can get encephalitis and get permanent brain damage. You can have permanent neurologic complications from getting measles. And now we know it’s in the community. We know it’s around us. We know that it’s spread through the air. It is the most infectious viral disease that we know of,” he said. The measles virus can remain in the air for up to two hours. Symptoms include high fever, cough, runny nose, and red or watery eyes. A rash can begin as flat red spots on the face and spread down the body, and small raised bumps may also appear. Doctors recommend all children receive two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. People who were previously vaccinated do not need a booster shot. The Oneida County Health Department is extending vaccination clinic hours in Utica and Rome. You can find information here. The Onondaga County Health Department offers vaccinations by appointment on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays. Find more information on Madison County's Immunization clinics for September and October here. An infant in Travis County has been diagnosed with measles, Austin Public Health announced Thursday. It is the county's second confirmed case of 2026. In a news release, local health officials stressed the importance of protecting from measles exposure by getting vaccinated for measles, mumps and rubella. The virus is highly contagious and can lead to severe complications. "Measles poses a serious risk, especially now that kids are heading back to school," said Dr. Desmar Walkes, Austin-Travis County Health Authority, in a news release. "Getting your MMR vaccine not only protects you but also your family, friends, classmates and coworkers." APH representatives said the patient, who was unvaccinated, had most likely been exposed to measles while traveling internationally and visited two local healthcare sites while infectious: Vik Complete Care Lakeway on Sept. 5 and the Texas Children's Pediatrics location on Del Rio Boulevard on Sept. 8. Those clinics are in the process of notifying patients who may have been exposed to the virus. APH said Texas Children's had already contacted all families who could be affected. Measles is spread by airborne transmission and can remain in the air for up to two hours. Typical measles symptoms include fever, cough, rash, eye irritation, runny nose and distinctive white spots inside the mouth. It may take up to two weeks for symptoms to appear after an exposure. The virus can also result in more severe issues, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain, and can lead to death. Another local measles case in an unvaccinated adult male was announced in May. Fresh Air Wild Card with Rachel Martin It's Been a Minute Embedded Get NPR+ More Podcasts & Shows Search Newsletters NPR Shop Get NPR+ Sign InPersonalize Your Experience Tiny Desk New Music Friday All Songs Considered Music Features Live Sessions About NPR Diversity Support Careers Press Ethics Worries about the CDC reliability hover over flu season The worst U.S. measles outbreak in decades is growing and flu season is imminent. Experts are fretting about federal health data reliability after the CDC questioned two Pennsylvania measles deaths. Health As diseases loom, CDC's response to measles deaths stirs fears about agency's reliability September 11, 202611:34 AM ET Heard on All Things Considered Rob Stein As diseases loom, CDC’s response to measles deaths stirs fears about agency’s reliability Listen· 4:044-Minute ListenPlaylist Toggle more options Download Embed Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5950002/nx-s1-9923393" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"> David J. Sencer CDC Museum at the Edward R. Roybal campus, the headquarters of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in Atlanta, Georgia. CDC is the national public health agency of the United States, under the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). hapabapa/Getty Images/iStock Editorial hide caption toggle caption hapabapa/Getty Images/iStock Editorial The worst measles resurgence in the U.S. in decades keeps growing. Vaccination rates keep falling. Flu, COVID-19, and RSV keep coming back. Against this backdrop, many public health experts are worried about the reliability of health information coming from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. "Red flag. Red alert," says Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, who resigned last year as the director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protest what he called political interference at the agency. Children's Health Trump and RFK Jr. try again to upend vaccines for kids Daskalakis and other independent public health authorities around the country are alarmed by how the CDC handled two deaths that Pennsylvania state officials recently blamed on measles. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. took the unprecedented step of questioning the deaths, and the CDC removed them from the agency's website. "When they raise doubt on the adjudication that a state may have made around a death, that is highly problematic," says Daskalakis. "This is dangerous." Usually, when someone dies from measles, the state where the tragedy happened determines the cause of death and reports the death to the CDC so the agency can alert the public, doctors and health officials around the country. The CDC usually defers to the state's determination. So Kennedy's public dispute with the state and the CDC's response is concerning for what it may mean for the relationship between states and federal health officials, who have to work closely to protect the public, Daskalakis and others say. That relationship has already become strained under the Trump administration. "What we have been seeing, that got amplified even more with these measles cases, is a breakdown in the coordination and trust between states and the federal government," says Dr. Anne Zink, a senior fellow at the Yale School of Public Health who previously served as Alaska's chief medical officer and president of the Association for State and Territorial Health Officers. "That to me is a significant concern. These partnerships are critical and essential to making us healthy and well." Zink and others also worry about whether the public, state and local health officials, doctors and others will be able to trust federal health data about measles as well as other diseases, such as flu, COVID-19 and RSV. Could CDC succumb to pressure to suppress information to minimize concerns about those diseases and the impact of falling immunization rates? Kennedy has long questioned vaccines. "We need to have good solid evidence-based national data. And I'm obviously concerned that it will happen again for other infectious diseases," says Dr. Georges Benjamin, who heads the American Public Health Association. "If it happens with flu and with COVID, the question is: Who can we rely on for the data on a national level. More people will get sick and more people because they won't know what to do. They won't know who to trust. And that is the problem here." Many also worry about what this means for the effectiveness of the new CDC director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, who recently took over after a tumultuous year that has left the CDC demoralized and diminished. Many hoped Schultz, a well-respected physician and attorney with solid public health experience, would restore the CDC's morale and credibility by pushing back against political pressure. But many say the way the CDC handled the Pennsylvania measles cases don't bode well for Schultz pushing back against political pressure. "We are seeing a pretty compromised CDC and a director who is at best facilitating non-scientific behavior and at worst colluding with non-scientific behavior," says Daskalakis. Others agree. "What the director should be doing instead of looking into these disease counts is responding to the outbreak itself," says Dr. Debra Houry, who resigned as the CDC's chief medical officer at the same time as Daskalakis for the same reasons. "I haven't heard from her talking about the importance of getting kindergarteners vaccinated when we're seeing declining rates. It's back to school time around the United States. We need her to step up publicly to talk about what can be done." Neither the CDC nor the Department of Health and Human Services responded to NPR's repeated requests for comment. records.content: Health & Fitness Measles Study Finds Low Vaccination Hotspots In Contra Costa County Researchers found seven low-vaccination clusters spanning eight Bay Area counties. CONTRA COSTA COUNTY, CA — Despite Northern California’s high overall measles vaccination rate, Kaiser Permanente researchers identified seven pockets where coverage fell below expected levels, including a sizeable portion of Sonoma County and a section of Napa County. The findings come as measles cases surge nationwide and vaccine skepticism drives federal policy. The study, published July 30 in JAMA Network Open, examined vaccination rates among 7-year-old Kaiser patients. Researchers found seven clusters of U.S. Census tracts that collectively recorded lower-than-expected coverage for measles-containing vaccines. Find out what's happening in Concordfor free with the latest updates from Patch. The clusters crossed eight counties in the North Bay, greater Sacramento area, and Fresno County. They covered 242 census tracts and included 25,803 children, representing 10.8% of the children in the study. Those areas recorded a combined vaccination rate of 94.6%. That is just below the vaccination rate necessary to establish herd immunity against measles. National health officials set that rate at 95%. Find out what's happening in Concordfor free with the latest updates from Patch. The study’s authors said the findings could help local health officials identify communities at heightened risk. Measles on the rise The research follows recent warnings that measles has regained ground domestically and globally. Measles was declared eliminated, but not eradicated, in the United States in 2000. That meant the virus no longer spread continuously within the country, although travelers could still carry it into the United States. During the first three months of 2024, health officials confirmed 58 cases across 17 states, including California — matching the total number of U.S. cases recorded during all of 2023. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said 93% of those cases were connected to international travel. Austria, the Philippines, Romania, and the United Kingdom were experiencing outbreaks at the time. California confirmed four cases by March 16, 2024, equaling its total for all of 2023. Hundreds of people that year faced possible exposure at UC Davis Medical Center after staff treated an infected child, according to Sacramento County Public Health. Officials also reported a possible exposure at an Alameda County restaurant in 2024. In June this year, a fifth case of measles was confirmed in Los Angeles County and health officials warned that members of the public may have been exposed at LAX and several other places. As of Aug. 31, California officials have confirmed 59 measles cases in the state. Despite the low rate of immunization, Sonoma County’s last confirmed case of measles was recorded in 2011. However, in January, Napa county officials recently reported the first case of measles diagnosed in a resident since 2012. On March 13 and 16, the measles virus was also detected in city of Napa wastewater through routine sampling, indicating the virus could again be present in the county. In the East Bay, Contra Costa Health notified the public about a measles case confirmed in late 2025, after the infected person visited several shops — including Macy's, Anthropologie and the Apple Store — in Lafayette and Walnut Creek while they were contagious. The CDC recommends two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, with the first administered between 12 and 15 months and the second between ages 4 and 6 or before a child starts school. The agency has also recommended vaccination for children 6 months and older who will travel internationally. An infected person can transmit measles to nine out of 10 unvaccinated people nearby. The virus spreads through infectious droplets and the air when a person breathes, coughs, or sneezes, and it can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for as long as two hours. Early symptoms include a high fever, cough, runny nose, and pink eye. A rash typically appears about 14 days after exposure. Infected people can transmit the virus from four days before the rash begins through four days afterward. Why did Dr. Vélez de Brown attribute the rise in measles cases to vaccination trends? topics: Measles Strong Memorial Hospital Monroe County Public health Emergency Department Rochester Vaccination Rochester-Finger Lakes Rochester, N.Y. — The Monroe County Department of Public Health is warning about a potential measles exposure at Strong Memorial Hospital. In a release Wednesday, the department said someone who tested positive for measles — and does not live in Monroe County — visited the hospital's emergency department between 11 p.m. Monday and 2 a.m. Tuesday, potentially exposing nearly 100 other people to the disease. The department said patients who visited Strong's emergency department during that time and don't have documented evidence of immunity are being contacted individually. Those people are being asked to monitor for signs and symptoms through Sept. 28 and seek medical immediately if they become ill. "It is such a small virus that it can hang out in the air in a space for two hours after a patient has left, and so there's no way to know for sure whether someone has been exposed to it until so many days later when they develop the disease," said Dr. Marielena Vélez de Brown, the county's public health commissioner. "If you don't get a call and you were registered, signed in as a patient, then that's probably good news," she added. "What we might not know specifically is the name of any companions who might have taken the patient." "So if you combine misinformation, fear-mongering concerns about made-up false claims associated with vaccines with folks' busy lives and being more mobile, the lower the number of people that have been vaccinated, the higher the risk that someone who is going to develop measles is then going to come in contact with someone who doesn't have that protection." The health department's release noted the two-dose measles, mumps and rubella vaccine series is safe and is 97% effective in preventing measles. Vélez de Brown said just one dose is 93% effective. Monroe County, which has a current MMR vaccination rate of 86%, has has not reported any measles cases since 2019. "There are years and years of data that it's very, very safe," Vélez de Brown said. "And so I would ask everyone in the community to follow our traditional schedule for vaccination." The U.S. eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. records.content: FILE – This undated image made available by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Feb. 4, 2015, shows an electron microscope image of a measles virus particle. (Cynthia Goldsmith/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, via AP, File) By Associated Press PUBLISHED: September 9, 2026 at 3:50 PM MDT | UPDATED: September 9, 2026 at 4:16 PM MDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... By MIKE STOBBE NEW YORK (AP) — The two measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania last month involved infants, and the virus itself caused one of the deaths, a Pennsylvania coroner confirmed Wednesday. Lancaster County’s coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, said he told the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention of his conclusions. CDC officials, however, have not said whether they will count either death as measles-associated, and the agency’s website still carries a disclaimer about them. Ivan Miller died on Aug. 14 shortly after his birth of a ruptured spleen, Diamantoni said. Mary Stoltzfus was 6 weeks old when she died Aug. 18 at her home. She was born with a genetic birth defect that left her highly vulnerable to an infection. A measles infection killed her, Diamantoni told The Associated Press. He said he was releasing the information in response to a state right-to-know law request by WPMT-TV, Fox 43. The causes of death differed Diamantoni’s office didn’t perform an autopsy on the girl. The cause of death was determined by the doctors caring for her, he said. She had been born with a condition called Amish lethal microcephaly that causes an unusually small head and underdeveloped brain. Children with the condition typically live 6 months or less. His office did autopsy the boy, and determined he died from a ruptured spleen. Exactly how and when that happened is still under investigation, Diamantoni said. The boy was infected with measles, which is listed on the death certificate as a contributing factor. But Diamantoni said measles did not contribute to what happened to the spleen, and that measles is noted only because it was considered “a significant condition” that the boy had at the time of death. Neither was old enough to be vaccinated; the first dose is typically given at around 1 year of age. The deaths have received outsized attention Details of the deaths have come under unusual national scrutiny and became the focus of a furious political battle between Pennsylvania’s Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro , and officials in Republican President Donald Trump’s administration. Pennsylvania officials announced the deaths last month, with Shapiro stressing that vaccinations could have averted the deaths. Soon after, U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. , a Trump administration appointee with a history of raising alarms about established vaccines, attacked Shapiro and suggested the deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” Kennedy’s statements echoed ones he made last year, when three measles-related deaths were recorded. Kennedy questioned whether one of the children who died was killed by measles. The health secretary oversees the CDC, and some public health experts have voiced concern about whether the CDC can still be counted on to post public health data that clashes with Kennedy’s worldview. “Frankly, the CDC is not to be trusted in sharing information,” Dr. Georges Benjamin, executive director of the American Public Health Association, told the AP last week. “People are questioning their motives.” CDC website still doesn’t show the deaths That worry was fueled by some unusual edits to the CDC’s measles webpage. At one point, the webpage noted two measles-associated deaths but then was changed to say that the CDC was not counting the two deaths until it reviewed additional information. The page , which was last updated Friday, now says, “CDC will update its reporting as additional information becomes available and relevant reviews are completed.” It still doesn’t reflect either Pennsylvania death. In a social media post last week, Kennedy acknowledged Diamantoni’s conclusion that one of the deaths was due to measles. Meanwhile, Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak continues to expand, with more than 620 cases across 37 counties this year, state officials said Wednesday. The U.S. eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Meanwhile, measles infections have been surging in recent years. In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status . (Cynthia Goldsmith/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, via AP, File) By Associated Press PUBLISHED: September 9, 2026 at 3:50 PM MDT | UPDATED: September 9, 2026 at 4:16 PM MDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... By MIKE STOBBE NEW YORK (AP) — The two measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania last month involved infants, and the virus itself caused one of the deaths, a Pennsylvania coroner confirmed Wednesday. Lancaster County’s coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, said he told the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention of his conclusions. CDC officials, however, have not said whether they will count either death as measles-associated, and the agency’s website still carries a disclaimer about them. Ivan Miller died on Aug. 14 shortly after his birth of a ruptured spleen, Diamantoni said. Mary Stoltzfus was 6 weeks old when she died Aug. 18 at her home. She was born with a genetic birth defect that left her highly vulnerable to an infection. A measles infection killed her, Diamantoni told The Associated Press. He said he was releasing the information in response to a state right-to-know law request by WPMT-TV, Fox 43. The causes of death differed Diamantoni’s office didn’t perform an autopsy on the girl. The cause of death was determined by the doctors caring for her, he said. She had been born with a condition called Amish lethal microcephaly that causes an unusually small head and underdeveloped brain. Children with the condition typically live 6 months or less. His office did autopsy the boy, and determined he died from a ruptured spleen. Exactly how and when that happened is still under investigation, Diamantoni said. The boy was infected with measles, which is listed on the death certificate as a contributing factor. But Diamantoni said measles did not contribute to what happened to the spleen, and that measles is noted only because it was considered “a significant condition” that the boy had at the time of death. Neither was old enough to be vaccinated; the first dose is typically given at around 1 year of age. The deaths have received outsized attention Details of the deaths have come under unusual national scrutiny and became the focus of a furious political battle between Pennsylvania’s Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, and officials in Republican President Donald Trump’s administration. Pennsylvania officials announced the deaths last month, with Shapiro stressing that vaccinations could have averted the deaths. Soon after, U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a Trump administration appointee with a history of raising alarms about established vaccines, attacked Shapiro and suggested the deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” Kennedy’s statements echoed ones he made last year, when three measles-related deaths were recorded. Kennedy questioned whether one of the children who died was killed by measles. The health secretary oversees the CDC, and some public health experts have voiced concern about whether the CDC can still be counted on to post public health data that clashes with Kennedy’s worldview. “Frankly, the CDC is not to be trusted in sharing information,” Dr. Georges Benjamin, executive director of the American Public Health Association, told the AP last week. “People are questioning their motives.” CDC website still doesn’t show the deaths That worry was fueled by some unusual edits to the CDC’s measles webpage. At one point, the webpage noted two measles-associated deaths but then was changed to say that the CDC was not counting the two deaths until it reviewed additional information. The page, which was last updated Friday, now says, “CDC will update its reporting as additional information becomes available and relevant reviews are completed.” It still doesn’t reflect either Pennsylvania death. In a social media post last week, Kennedy acknowledged Diamantoni’s conclusion that one of the deaths was due to measles. Meanwhile, Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak continues to expand, with more than 620 cases across 37 counties this year, state officials said Wednesday. The U.S. eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Meanwhile, measles infections have been surging in recent years. In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status. records.content: × Web Image Sort by Relevance Date Home News Local News Booking Report Letters to the Editor Obituaries California U.S. & World Politics Advertising Specials Senior News Fire Call Log Fire News Advertise Contact Us American Academy of Pediatrics Offers Guidance on Managing Infants with Congenital Measles as Disease Outbreaks Rise Details Last Updated: Wednesday, 09 September 2026 03:45 Published: Wednesday, 09 September 2026 05:11 Measles is now rapidly spreading in some communities with low vaccination rates, putting newborns at risk September 9, 2026 - ITASCA, IL— The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), citing growing measles outbreaks nationwide and limited guidance available to pediatricians, has developed a new tool to help physicians care for infants exposed to or infected with measles. Image by StockSnap from Pixabay AAP infectious disease experts developed a frequently asked questions document, available in the AAP's Red Book: 2024-2027 Report of the Committee on Infectious Diseases online. The FAQ addresses prevention, diagnosis and management of measles in babies born to mothers who were infected with measles during pregnancy. “Our goal is to help pediatricians care for newborns with congenital measles based on the existing evidence,” said AAP Chief Medical Officer Lee Beers, MD, FAAP. “While congenital measles was previously an uncommon condition and therefore the evidence is somewhat limited, this is an urgent need for pediatricians caring for patients in an active outbreak.” Two infants recently died from measles-associated illness in Pennsylvania, where 577 cases had been reported as of Sept. 4. None of those who contracted the disease had been fully vaccinated. There are now outbreaks of measles in many areas of the country, including among pregnant women who have never been vaccinated or infected with measles. As of Sept. 3, 2026, the CDC had reported 3,134 confirmed measles cases in the United States. The resurgence of this highly contagious disease marks a stark contrast to 2000, when measles was declared eliminated in the United States. “Measles, especially in babies, is not just as simple as getting a rash and it going away,” said Pia Pannaraj, MD, MPH, FAAP, a member of the AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases and a pediatrics professor at the University of California, San Diego. “It can have long-term consequences, including severe secondary infections as well as neurological complications down the road.” Because scientific evidence continues to evolve as new cases emerge, the AAP notes that the FAQ will likely require ongoing review and updates. The authors cited existing case reports and data that informed their work and responses to questions. They note in the FAQ where the data is limited, especially as measles during pregnancy used to be rare and can be prevented with routine childhood vaccinations. The AAP estimates that approximately 25% to 30% of infants born to mothers who contract measles in the days just before delivery may also become infected. Newborns with congenital measles can experience a wide range of outcomes, from no symptoms to classic measles rash, severe multi-organ disease or death. Infants with congenital measles are also at increased risk of developing subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare and progressive inflammatory brain disease that typically appears years after infection and is almost always fatal. Infants may show no symptoms at birth but still begin to show signs of the disease within months or a few years later, Dr. Pannaraj said. “It's important the families are aware so they can watch for any missing milestones.” Vaccination before pregnancy remains the safest and most effective way to prevent measles infection because the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy. AAP recommends that children should routinely receive two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine at 12 months, and a second dose between ages 4 to 6. The AAP also recommends earlier vaccination in special circumstances. “Many providers who have never seen measles except for the textbooks now need to look out for how to identify measles in their patients and what to do to protect them,” Dr. Pannaraj said. "This is an issue that isn't going away.” The American Academy of Pediatrics is an organization of 67,000 primary care pediatricians, pediatric medical subspecialists and pediatric surgical specialists dedicated to the health, safety and well-being of infants, children, adolescents and young adults. I am 18 or older, or my parent or guardian is submitting this for me. Read the full terms Send Photo A suspected case of measles in Cayuga County has now been confirmed through laboratory testing. The Cayuga County Health Department announced Tuesday that the case involving a county resident was confirmed after initially being reported as a suspected case on Friday. Health officials say the confirmed case follows other recent measles cases identified across the Finger Lakes region. The Health Department continues to work with the infected individual while conducting contact tracing and a case investigation. People identified as close contacts will be notified that they may have been exposed to the measles virus. Post-exposure treatment has been offered and administered to unvaccinated members of the individual’s household and other identified close contacts. County health officials are urging residents to make sure they are vaccinated against measles. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine are considered safe and effective at preventing measles infection. The vaccine is available through most primary care providers. People without a healthcare provider or health insurance can contact the Cayuga County Health Department to schedule a vaccination appointment. By Sun-Times Wire The Chicago Department of Public Health warned of a potential measles exposure at Union Station in August. Kane County health officials also confirmed its second case of measles. AP file SHARE COPY LINK Share CLOSE Twitter Facebook Bluesky Email Reddit Flipboard An out-of-state domestic traveler with a confirmed case of measles passed through Union Station in the West Loop late last month, Chicago health authorities announced Thursday. The stricken traveler was at Union Station in the 200 block of South Canal Street on Thursday, Aug. 27th after 8:00 p.m. through Friday, Aug. 28th, according to a statement from the Chicago Department of Public Health. CDPH didn’t provide a time for the traveler’s departure. The exact date and time of exposure are unknown at this time. If more information becomes available, CDPH will update the exposure location posting on its website. A second measles case was also confirmed in Kane County Thursday, weeks after the area’s first confirmed case, according to health officials. The person was vaccinated against measles and in contact with the first case, which was first reported Aug. 24, according to the Kane County Health Department. While a vaccination protects against measles, breakthrough cases, where a vaccinated person can get measles, still occur, health officials said. People who are vaccinated and develop measles are generally less likely to experience severe illness or complications and may be less likely to transmit the virus. The first confirmed case in Kane County included two possible exposure locations: Kaneland High School in Maple Park on Aug. 18, during the school day. Next Generation Pediatric Clinic in South Elgin on Aug, 21, between 12:30 p.m. and 4 p.m. As of Thursday, there were 11 reported measles cases in the state, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health. It delivers clear answers and real-time content based on what people are reading now — showcasing various stories from the USA TODAY Network that highlight not just what happened, but why it matters. Please reference surfaced articles to validate AI summary Explore DeeperDive Ask USA TODAY anything What genetic condition made Mary Stoltzfus vulnerable to measles? Why did Robert F. Kennedy Jr. request removal of Pennsylvania deaths from CDC data? Why do public health experts criticize Kennedy's vaccine policies? A Pennsylvania coroner confirmed Wednesday that the state's two measles-related deaths last month both involved infants, and that the virus caused one of the deaths. Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, Lancaster County’s coroner, said Ivan Miller died Aug. 14 shortly after his birth of a ruptured spleen, and 6-week-old Mary Stoltzfus died Aug. 18 at her home from a measles infection, according to the Associated Press and The Washington Post. A genetic birth defect called Amish lethal microcephaly, which causes a small head and underdeveloped brain, left Stoltzfus highly vulnerable to an infection, he explained to the outlets. Diamantoni said he released the information in response to a state right-to-know law request by WPMT-TV, Fox 43. USA TODAY reached out to the coroner's office for comment. Diamantoni’s office didn’t perform an autopsy on Stoltzfus, so the cause of death was determined by her doctors, he told the AP. Diamantoni’s office did autopsy Miller, and determined that he died of a ruptured spleen. While Miller was infected with measles − which is listed on the death certificate as a contributing factor − Diamantoni said measles did not contribute to what happened to the spleen, and that the virus is noted only because it was considered “a significant condition” at the time of death. Neither was old enough to be vaccinated, as the first dose is typically given around age 1. The political divide over measles deaths These deaths have come under national scrutiny and political debate. Last month, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked for the two deaths reported by Pennsylvania’s health department to be removed from the CDC’s national tally of measles cases, questioning whether the virus was the cause. CDC staffers had already accepted the state’s characterization of the deaths as linked to measles before Kennedy's request. Last week, Kennedy acknowledged that measles caused the recent death of one Pennsylvania infant, citing information from the county coroner, but suggested that the federal government would not yet recognize the fatality in official data amid a fast-growing national outbreak. Public health experts said the move amounted to extraordinary political interference in the authority of a state health department and an effort to minimize the risks of the highly infectious virus. Measles cases hit highest level in more than 30 years U.S. measles cases have hit their highest level in more than three decades under President Donald Trump and Kennedy, his top health official and a long-time vaccine skeptic. Kennedy has promoted the idea that vaccines, including the combined measles, mumps and rubella shot, are more dangerous than the diseases they prevent, despite decades of scientific evidence that the shots save lives. Leading medical organizations say that Kennedy’s statements about vaccines and his policies as health secretary, including efforts to reduce the number of government-recommended childhood immunizations, have increased vaccine hesitancy, making outbreaks harder to curb. Diamantoni’s office didn’t perform an autopsy on Stoltzfus, so the cause of death was determined by her doctors, he told the AP. Diamantoni’s office did autopsy Miller, and determined that he died of a ruptured spleen. While Miller was infected with measles − which is listed on the death certificate as a contributing factor − Diamantoni said measles did not contribute to what happened to the spleen, and that the virus is noted only because it was considered “a significant condition” at the time of death. Neither was old enough to be vaccinated, as the first dose is typically given around age 1. The political divide over measles deaths These deaths have come under national scrutiny and political debate. Last month, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked for the two deaths reported by Pennsylvania’s health department to be removed from the CDC’s national tally of measles cases, questioning whether the virus was the cause. CDC staffers had already accepted the state’s characterization of the deaths as linked to measles before Kennedy's request. Last week, Kennedy acknowledged that measles caused the recent death of one Pennsylvania infant, citing information from the county coroner, but suggested that the federal government would not yet recognize the fatality in official data amid a fast-growing national outbreak. Public health experts said the move amounted to extraordinary political interference in the authority of a state health department and an effort to minimize the risks of the highly infectious virus. Measles cases hit highest level in more than 30 years U.S. measles cases have hit their highest level in more than three decades under President Donald Trump and Kennedy, his top health official and a long-time vaccine skeptic. Kennedy has promoted the idea that vaccines, including the combined measles, mumps and rubella shot, are more dangerous than the diseases they prevent, despite decades of scientific evidence that the shots save lives. Leading medical organizations say that Kennedy’s statements about vaccines and his policies as health secretary, including efforts to reduce the number of government-recommended childhood immunizations, have increased vaccine hesitancy, making outbreaks harder to curb. records.content: Health & Fitness Measles Study Finds Low Vaccination Hotspots In Napa County Researchers found seven low-vaccination clusters spanning eight counties, including Napa, Sonoma, Sacramento-area, and Fresno communities. NAPA COUNTY, CA — Despite a high overall measles vaccination rate, Kaiser Permanente researchers identified seven pockets where coverage fell below expected levels, including a sizeable portion of Sonoma County and a section of Napa County. The findings come as measles cases surge nationwide and vaccine skepticism drives federal policy. The study, published July 30 in JAMA Network Open, examined vaccination rates among 7-year-old Kaiser patients. Researchers found seven clusters of U.S. Census tracts that collectively recorded lower-than-expected coverage for measles-containing vaccines. Find out what's happening in Napa Valleyfor free with the latest updates from Patch. The clusters crossed eight counties in the North Bay, greater Sacramento area, and Fresno County. They covered 242 census tracts and included 25,803 children, representing 10.8% of the children in the study. Those areas recorded a combined vaccination rate of 94.6%. That is just below the vaccination rate necessary to establish herd immunity against measles. National health officials set that rate at 95%. Find out what's happening in Napa Valleyfor free with the latest updates from Patch. The study’s authors said the findings could help local health officials identify communities at heightened risk. Measles on the rise The research follows recent warnings that measles has regained ground domestically and globally. Measles was declared eliminated, but not eradicated, in the United States in 2000. That meant the virus no longer spread continuously within the country, although travelers could still carry it into the United States. During the first three months of 2024, health officials confirmed 58 cases across 17 states, including California — matching the total number of U.S. cases recorded during all of 2023. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said 93% of those cases were connected to international travel. Austria, the Philippines, Romania, and the United Kingdom were experiencing outbreaks at the time. California confirmed four cases by March 16, 2024, equaling its total for all of 2023. Hundreds of people that year faced possible exposure at UC Davis Medical Center after staff treated an infected child, according to Sacramento County Public Health. Officials also reported a possible exposure at an Alameda County restaurant in 2024. In June this year, a fifth case of measles was confirmed in Los Angeles County and health officials warned that members of the public may have been exposed at LAX and several other places. As of Aug. 31, California officials have confirmed 59 measles cases in the state. Despite the low rate of immunization, Sonoma County’s last confirmed case of measles was recorded in 2011. However, in January, Napa county officials recently reported the first case of measles diagnosed in a resident since 2012. On March 13 and 16, the measles virus was also detected in city of Napa wastewater through routine sampling, indicating the virus could again be present in the county. In the East Bay, Contra Costa Health notified the public about a measles case confirmed in late 2025, after the infected person visited several shops — including Macy's, Anthropologie and the Apple Store — in Lafayette and Walnut Creek while they were contagious. The CDC recommends two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, with the first administered between 12 and 15 months and the second between ages 4 and 6 or before a child starts school. The agency has also recommended vaccination for children 6 months and older who will travel internationally. An infected person can transmit measles to nine out of 10 unvaccinated people nearby. The virus spreads through infectious droplets and the air when a person breathes, coughs, or sneezes, and it can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for as long as two hours. Early symptoms include a high fever, cough, runny nose, and pink eye. A rash typically appears about 14 days after exposure. Infected people can transmit the virus from four days before the rash begins through four days afterward. Check your local health department for the latest measles cases, outbreaks, and exposure notices in your county. Get more local news delivered straight to your inbox. Please reference surfaced articles to validate AI summary Explore DeeperDive Full Summary A measles outbreak tied to an Atlanta daycare has grown to eight confirmed cases, bringing Georgia's total to 17 in 2026 and surpassing the previous year's numbers, while nationwide cases exceed 3,000. A measles outbreak linked to an Atlanta area daycare continues to grow as three more cases were confirmed by public health officials. The Georgia Department of Public Health announced the total number of confirmed cases linked to the outbreak now stood at eight, as of Sept. 4. The state of Georgia has now passed the total number of measles cases in 2025, mirroring a 35-year high of measles cases seen across the country. The Atlanta cases were all confirmed in children who were not yet vaccinated or who had not been fully vaccinated, meaning they had not yet received a second dose of the MMR vaccine. Here's what to know about measles in Georgia. How many measles cases have there been in Georgia in 2026? As of Sept. 3, a total of 14 measles cases have been confirmed across the state of Georgia, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which is headquartered in Atlanta. The daycare outbreak in Atlanta would add an additional three cases to the total, which was not yet included in the CDC's data, bringing the actual total to 17 cases. There have now been more cases of measles by September of 2026 than in all of 2025 in Georgia. There were 10 total measles cases in Georgia in 2025. There are now more than 3,000 confirmed cases nationally, as of Sept. 4, rising above the roughly 2,200 cases seen across the United States last year. The vast majority of cases are among unvaccinated individuals, ranging in age from 5 years old to older than 20 years old. There have been 38 outbreaks in 2026, which includes groups of three or more cases stemming from one area, according to the CDC. Is measles contagious? Measles is a virus that is considered "very contagious" by health officials, and can spread through the air from coughs or sneezes as well as on surfaces. The measles virus can survive on surfaces for as long as two hours after an infected person has already left the area. That's why places like daycares or other school settings can be perfect incubators for measles outbreaks. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends the MMR vaccine — which is used to prevent measles, mumps and rubella — for all children. But, children are recommended to be vaccinated with their first dose between the ages of 12 and 15 months, and then their second dose isn't until between the ages of 4 and 6 years old. While the first dose means a child is largely protected from the infections, a second dose increases protection. What are symptoms of measles? Symptoms will start to appear between seven and 14 days after someone has been exposed to the virus, and includes fever, cough, runny nose and watery eyes. A rash of red spots also appears across your body, typically starting around your head. If you believe you or your child may be experiencing measles symptoms, contact a health care provider right away. records.content: 24/7 LiveChicago & Suburban Cook Co.North SuburbsWest SuburbsSouth SuburbsNW Indiana 78° Measles Officials warn of potential measles exposure at Chicago's Union Station Chicago health officials are investigating a potential measles exposure. ByMaher Kawash and ABC7 Chicago Digital Team Friday, September 11, 2026 1:10AM Share CHICAGO (WLS) -- Chicago health officials are investigating a potential measles exposure involving an out-of-state traveler who spent nearly 24 hours in the city after arriving by train. ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch At the same time, Kane County health leaders are also investigating a second measles case this summer involving a vaccinated individual. The Chicago Department of Public Health said a person traveling from Sedalia, Missouri, arrived at Union Station on Aug. 27 at about 10:30 p.m. and stayed overnight in Chicago before returning to Union Station on Aug. 28 at about 9 p.m. to travel to Rochester, New York. The department is working to contact people who may have been exposed. Health officials said it could take up to three weeks for infected individuals to develop symptoms. Dr. Alfredo Mena Lora, an infectious disease specialist at St. Anthony Hospital, said people who may have been exposed should monitor themselves for symptoms. "In general, what you should expect is within a week or two, and the longest stretch is three weeks, you can develop a cough, a fever and a rash," Dr. Mena Lora said. RELATED | New map shows how to spot the measles risk level in your ZIP code The most recent measles exposure investigation previously reported by the Chicago Department of Public Health involved an international traveler passing through O'Hare International Airport in late June. In Kane County, health officials are investigating what they describe as their second measles exposure this summer. Suburban officials said the latest case is considered a breakthrough case because the person had already been vaccinated. Michael Isaacson, executive director of the Kane County Health Department, said officials were not surprised to identify another case after an earlier investigation. "We had our first case at the end of August with that person we had over 1,600 contacts we identified, so we're not surprised to see another case. It's a little surprising that this case is fully vaccinated but that's not unheard of," Isaacson said. The Kane County Health Department said roughly 4 to 5% of people diagnosed with measles nationwide had been vaccinated. Officials said vaccinated individuals are generally less likely to experience severe symptoms and continued to urge vaccination, particularly for children. Dr. Mena Lora said measles remains highly contagious but preventable through vaccination. "It is very concerning this is a highly contagious condition which means if you're not vaccinated and exposed to somebody then the chances of you getting the condition is over 90 percent. It's a very infectious condition, but at the same time very preventable," Dr. Mena Lora said. Health experts said increasing vaccine hesitancy in recent years has contributed to a rise in measles cases. Isaacson pointed to growing case counts nationwide despite the availability of effective vaccines. "This is a very rare disease because we have such effective vaccines were seeing across the country cases continue to go up. I believe nationwide were over 3,100 cases already, and last year we had about 2,200 cases as opposed to 20 years ago the whole country only had 55 cases," he said. Kane County health officials said people exposed to measles are generally expected to quarantine for 21 days. However, officials said individuals who are vaccinated and have immunity typically do not need to quarantine. Report a correction or typo Copyright © 2026 WLS-TV. All Rights Reserved. Anthony Museum & House Expansion Rochester Gas Prices Pet of the Week Do The Right Thing ESL Heart of Service Award Careers × Watch Now: News10NBC at 7 County health officials warn about possible measles exposure at Strong’s emergency department Evan Bourtis, Adelisa Badžić News10NBC Updated: September 10, 2026 - 1:06 AM Published: September 9, 2026 - 1:18 PM Measles graphic (file image) ROCHESTER, N.Y. — A person with measles visited Strong Memorial Hospital’s emergency department earlier this month, potentially exposing about 100 people to the highly contagious virus. The infected person, who was not vaccinated and is not a Monroe County resident, was in the adult or pediatric emergency departments from 11 p.m. on Sept. 7 through 2 a.m. on Sept. 8, Monroe County health officials Wednesday. RELATED: More measles cases confirmed in Steuben County, health official weighs in on staying safe “Measles is a highly contagious respiratory disease, so it’s caused by a virus that spread by direct contact with either nasal secretions or from the throat,” said Dr. Marielena Vélez de Brown, the county’s commissioner for public health. “It is such a small virus that it can hang out in the air in a space for two hours after a patient has left.” The Monroe County Department of Public Health is reviewing records of patients who were in the emergency department during the exposure period. Hospital or county health officials will contact anyone who was there without documented evidence of immunity. Anyone who was in the emergency department during that time should monitor themselves for symptoms through Sept. 28. The department’s phone number is 585-753-5555. “If you start to feel ill, do not go straight into the doctors,” Dr. Vélez de Brown said. “This is the one time when I would ask, definitely contact your healthcare provider or call the emergency department, but let them know the concern that you were potentially in one of these two locations in recent weeks where we’ve had exposures.” Tracking measles cases locally Measles is a very contagious respiratory disease, caused by a virus and spread by contact with nasal or throat secretions of infected people. The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles outbreak in 35 years, and News10NBC has been tracking cases locally. Here are the latest numbers: At least 10 confirmed cases in Steuben County At least five confirmed cases in Seneca County At least two confirmed cases in Ontario County At least one confirmed case in Yates County In addition, a person infected with measles traveled through the Louise M. Slaughter Train Station in Rochester on Saturday, Aug. 29. Monroe County health officials say the person wasn’t a county resident, but may have exposed others. The risk of getting measles is low for people who have gotten vaccinated or have had measles in the past. You can learn more about getting vaccinated here. Symptoms of measles Measles symptoms usually appear 10 to 12 days after exposure but may take as long as 21 days. Symptoms typically appear in two stages. The first stage includes a runny nose, cough, and a slight fever. In addition, eyes may become reddened and small bluish-white spots, surrounded by a red area, may appear in the mouth. The second stage includes a red blotchy rash lasting five to six days. The rash usually begins on the face and then spreads downward and outward, reaching the hands and feet. If you have measles symptoms, call your doctor before going to a clinic, so they can prevent you from exposing others. “The best way that the community can protect itself is by vaccination,” Dr. Vélez de Brown said. “One MMR vaccine is calculated to be 93% effective in preventing a person from developing measles if they have been exposed. And then the combination of two valid MMR vaccines is up to 97% effective.” Monroe County’s vaccination rate is 86% of children having had one dose by two years of age, down from 87% in January 2025. Health officials recommend children receive the MMR vaccine at their first birthday and fourth birthday. For families traveling, officials recommend children can receive the MMR vaccine as early as six months of age, though this does not replace the need for vaccines at one year and four years. “We are seeing vaccine rates dropping across the country,” Dr. Vélez de Brown added. “Even here, amongst a very well-educated, well-informed population, we’re seeing the trend of slowly decreasing rates of folks being vaccinated.” Again, anyone with concerns about potential exposure can call the Monroe County Department of Public Health at 585-753-5555. Residents of other counties should contact their local health departments. MessageFacebookMessengerRedditWhatsAppCopy LinkEmailXShare ✓ Thanks for sharing! More

Public Health Coroner Confirms Measles Killed Pennsylvania Infant As Federal Count Still Lags Federal health officials have not added either of the two infant deaths reported last month to national totals You can still access 2 more articles for free. - A Pennsylvania coroner says measles killed one of two infants who died in the state last month - The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has not yet counted either death in national totals - Pennsylvania's measles outbreak has grown to more than 620 cases across 37 counties this year THURSDAY, Sept. 10, 2026 (HealthDay News) — A Pennsylvania coroner has confirmed that measles killed one of two infants who died in the state last month, but federal health officials still are not counting either death in the national measles tally. Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, the coroner in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, said Wednesday that he has shared his conclusions with the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Associated Press reports. Mary Stoltzfus was 6 weeks old when she died at home Aug. 18. She was born with Amish lethal microcephaly, a rare inherited condition that causes an unusually small head and an underdeveloped brain. Children born with it typically live six months or less. The condition left her with very little defense against infection, and a measles infection killed her, Diamantoni told AP News. His office did not perform an autopsy on the girl. Her cause of death was determined by the doctors treating her. Ivan Miller died Aug. 14, shortly after he was born, of a ruptured spleen. Diamantoni's office did perform an autopsy on the boy, he said. Exactly how and when the spleen ruptured is still under investigation. The boy was infected with measles, and the virus is listed on his death certificate as a contributing factor. But Diamantoni said measles played no role in the spleen injury and is noted only because it was a significant condition the boy had when he died. The first dose of measles vaccine is usually given around age 1, meaning neither infant was old enough to receive it for protection from the virus's spread. The CDC's measles webpage briefly listed two measles-associated deaths, then was changed to say the agency would not count them until it reviewed more information. The page, last updated Friday, still does not reflect either death. The deaths also set off a public clash between Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat who said vaccination could have prevented them, and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who suggested the deaths might have been made up, reports AP News. Kennedy has a long history of vaccine skepticism. Both deaths are documented in official records, including an autopsy in one case, and Kennedy acknowledged the coroner's measles finding in a social media post last week. The dispute has left some public health leaders uneasy about federal data. "Frankly, the CDC is not to be trusted in sharing information," Dr. Georges Benjamin, executive director of the American Public Health Association, told AP News. He said people are questioning the agency's motives. Meanwhile, the state's outbreak keeps growing. As of Wednesday, Pennsylvania had recorded more than 620 measles cases in 37 counties this year, state officials said. The U.S. once halted the routine spread of measles within its borders. However, vaccination rates have since slipped below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. International health officials plan to meet in November to decide whether the United States has lost its measles-free status. More information Visit the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for more information about measles vaccination. SOURCE: AP News, Sept. 9, 2026 Babies younger than 1 year are too young for the measles vaccine, so their protection depends on the people around them. People should make sure everyone in their household is up to date on their shots. www.healthday.com

Health officials in Kane County also confirmed a second measles case for the area. By Sun-Times Wire Sept 10, 2026, 6:44pm UTC The Chicago Department of Public Health warned of a potential measles exposure at Union Station in August. Kane County health officials also confirmed its second case of measles. AP file SHARE COPY LINK Share CLOSE Twitter Facebook Bluesky Email Reddit Flipboard An out-of-state domestic traveler with a confirmed case of measles passed through Union Station in the West Loop late last month, Chicago health authorities announced Thursday. The stricken traveler was at Union Station in the 200 block of South Canal Street on Thursday, Aug. 27th after 8:00 p.m. through Friday, Aug. 28th, according to a statement from the Chicago Department of Public Health. CDPH didn’t provide a time for the traveler’s departure. The exact date and time of exposure are unknown at this time. If more information becomes available, CDPH will update the exposure location posting on its website. A second measles case was also confirmed in Kane County Thursday, weeks after the area’s first confirmed case, according to health officials. The person was vaccinated against measles and in contact with the first case, which was first reported Aug. 24, according to the Kane County Health Department. While a vaccination protects against measles, breakthrough cases, where a vaccinated person can get measles, still occur, health officials said. People who are vaccinated and develop measles are generally less likely to experience severe illness or complications and may be less likely to transmit the virus. The first confirmed case in Kane County included two possible exposure locations: Kaneland High School in Maple Park on Aug. 18, during the school day. Next Generation Pediatric Clinic in South Elgin on Aug, 21, between 12:30 p.m. and 4 p.m. As of Thursday, there were 11 reported measles cases in the state, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health. records.content: FOX 2 Possible measles exposure reported at Missouri train station Alex Barton 2 days ago JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. — Missouri health officials are warning of a possible measles exposure at the Sedalia train station after a Missouri resident confirmed to have the virus got on a train headed to Chicago on Aug. 27. According to the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, the person boarded Amtrak Train 318 at the Sedalia station while going through Pettis County to another destination. The person is not a resident of Pettis County. Officials said details about the possible exposure are limited at this time. More information will be provided if it becomes available. People who may have been exposed should monitor themselves for measles symptoms for three weeks after the exposure date and contact their local public health agency if symptoms develop. Measles is a highly contagious viral illness. One person with measles can spread it to as many as nine out of 10 people near them who are unvaccinated or don’t have natural immunity, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Symptoms usually consist of fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes. A rash typically pops up three to five days after the initial symptoms and usually starts on the face near the hairline before spreading down the body. The virus can spread through direct contact or through the air when a person who’s infected breathes, coughs, or sneezes. It can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area, DHSS says. People who think they might have measles should isolate themselves, then call their healthcare provider before going to a doctor’s office. Patients should tell their provider they are concerned about measles and follow instructions for getting tested and treated without exposing other people. Measles can cause serious complications like pneumonia and encephalitis, and can be deadly. The best way to prevent measles is vaccination. Two doses of a measles vaccine gives about 97% protection against the infection. The CDC and Missouri DHSS recommend kids get their first dose at 12 to 15 months old and a second dose at 4 to 6 years old. Unvaccinated adults can also get a catch-up MMR vaccine. Measles can be especially dangerous for pregnant women, their unborn children, and babies who are too young to be vaccinated. More information about measles and MMR vaccination rates is available through the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services. Ad Your Privacy Choices
